sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Paid growth is not a unanimous starting prescription. McGarry usually wants content-market fit first, describing approximately 1,000–10,000 subscribers and generally 5,000–10,000 before paid growth and monetization. Publishing on an appropriate social platform helps establish that demand, although fast monetization can justify earlier spending. Sharpe argues that funded operators with buying skill, strong editorial, and a revenue model should not automatically spend months on labor-intensive organic growth. Lookout reportedly acquired more than 90% of its audience through paid channels while maintaining 58%+ opens and 12% unique click-through. Sharpe would rather put a growth-worker-equivalent salary into Facebook acquisition than continually produce Reddit posts, tweets, or guest posts, but agrees that resource-poor operators need organic routes and unvalidated ideas should not be scaled. Brogan treats this as a resource-allocation choice: time, capital, skills, platform knowledge, goals, and horizon determine the channel. Manual cross-promotions were a poor use of their limited time, yet can suit time-rich publishers. Wanda Zelaya takes a firmer organic position after rejection from paid recommendations, welcoming reciprocal promotion and accepting slower growth. These are materially different operating preferences, not interchangeable claims that every newsletter must either buy readers immediately or avoid advertising entirely. [uVhFrwe935U @ 00:03:53] [7x3W0vKolWY @ 00:18:37] [cGtTorgyz9I @ 00:09:23] [bHypgQE6iLY @ 00:07:14]

Onboarding frequency and page design contain genuine tactical tension. Nicholls's revenue masterclass favors two to five emails during the first day or couple of days, including an offer after one or two hours and later reminders of recommendations or resources. They would rather lose an unsuitable reader than let a suitable reader forget the publication. McGarry does not think everyone needs seven emails in seven days; a weekly publication may need a three-to-five-part sequence, and editorial quality comes first. McGarry also suggests asking for roughly two inbox actions, such as replying or moving the message to primary. Nicholls rejects making primary-tab instructions the thank-you page's main job, preferring a mystery gift or resource that motivates an email click or reply. On landing pages, Holm recommends testimonials, writer introductions, example content, and faces when appropriate. Max reports improvement after removing sprawling explanations, schedules, testimonials, and logos in favor of immediate benefits, concise proof, and 'Continue.' Max explicitly says a visual change that helped their own page may not help another. Both page playbooks prioritize the reader's reason to act, but they do not prescribe the same collection of page elements or the same volume of explanatory material. [q1jLTPNMaCY @ 00:35:05] [uVhFrwe935U @ 00:46:01] [XnLPTqyukUI @ 00:24:36] [wW2Mpe3uxT8 @ 00:23:13]

Local newsletters also split on product, personality, and monetization. Lookout's Sharpe foregrounds deeper reporting, paid membership, and a transferable brand; Ryan Sneddon's Naptown Scoop is positive, activity-oriented, and heavily advertising-funded, with non-advertising revenue probably below 2%. Sneddon puts a recognizable person into the community, attends events, and reports continued weekly growth after stopping Facebook spending almost two years before the interview. Referrals account for approximately 20% of the list, but Sneddon does not know an equally fast replacement for Facebook when town-specific acquisition is required. Nicholls's partner-program masterclass agrees that geographically broad networks are weak acquisition sources for local publications; local businesses, readers, influencers, and ambassadors are better recruitment targets. The same local publication can still earn by recommending suitable national newsletters. Jen Ransom argues for a different business altogether: rank simple local lead-generation websites, describing three weeks to six months to rank and organic traffic without paid-ad expense. That contrasts with Ransom's description of email affiliate arbitrage, where bought traffic drives purchases of offers promoted by competing affiliates. Ransom favors the search-led alternative, whereas the newsletter operators build recurring editorial relationships and monetize through memberships, advertisers, referrals, and adjacent offers. Their products and acquisition constraints are different. [7x3W0vKolWY @ 00:29:41] [55VTgJoSWco @ 00:24:36] [i_xgpz4ZZB8 @ 00:24:00] [6sEWUIZ-3R0 @ 00:04:48]

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Admission is a real operational bottleneck in Zelaya's account. After a couple of months on Kit and five weekly newsletters, Zelaya applied for paid recommendations, answered a follow-up request, and sent four editions when three were requested. They report a same-day rejection, followed by support declining to disclose specific criteria or internal decision processes. The reported response also said rejection was final and reapplication unavailable. Zelaya wanted a subscriber target, open-rate target, or other actionable improvement criterion and says earlier disclosure would have changed when they applied. Nicholls describes SparkLoop's network differently from the buyer's side: manual publisher vetting and restricted access are part of a quality cycle intended to attract better publishers and higher-paying buyers. Sakamoto's Beehiiv demonstration reaches a visible, working widget; its endpoint is installation and syncing, not a demonstrated referral payment. Zelaya still endorses free creator recommendations and remains complimentary about Kit while objecting to the application experience. Their separate story about someone spending over $20,000 on poor leads is secondhand, not Zelaya's own advertising loss. Keep that distinction attached to the complaint: the firsthand event is rejection and the support exchange, while the acquisition-quality accusation comes from another person's account. [bHypgQE6iLY @ 00:01:43] [pbmgkJeKEGc @ 00:11:58] [u87gia-3VVo @ 00:02:34] [bHypgQE6iLY @ 00:07:14]

Audience attention does not automatically become product sales. Max's $200 course sold to approximately three people despite roughly 50,000 social followers and a prelaunch campaign. That disappointment preceded the pivot to an advertising-funded newsletter and the reported $12,000–$25,000 monthly ad revenue at 10,000 subscribers. Max explicitly warns that those historical economics do not translate directly to the later 325,000-reader audience. Spector reports another mismatch: conventional sponsor-network advertisements performed worse than their one-sentence weekday format, leading Spector to require the preferred format with sponsor approval and decline incompatible advertisers. The two accounts show failed offers and failed packaging, not merely a need for more addresses. Ransom adds a separate cost and dependency critique of affiliate arbitrage: stated training prices include $39,995 for six months, $49,995 for one year, and $99,995 for VIP, alongside a 50/50 profit share for 24 months. Ransom also warns that affiliates can promote identical products, rivals may write stronger copy, parent companies can change contracts or discontinue offers, and links can be hijacked. Those are Ransom's reported risks, rather than losses Ransom personally demonstrates. Max and Spector's operational reversals remain concrete: change the revenue model or advertising presentation when the existing offer does not perform. [wW2Mpe3uxT8 @ 00:07:16] [KrUPlyUxncE @ 00:20:12] [6sEWUIZ-3R0 @ 00:01:08] [6sEWUIZ-3R0 @ 00:03:04]

Production and sales capacity can become tighter constraints than acquisition. Sneddon abandoned the ambition to personally build 100 publications after confronting the difficulty of finding deeply local operators; the revised plan emphasized teaching and roughly ten to twenty partnerships. Naptown's own workflow also exposed a verification failure: a Sunday-written Navy football schedule bypassed primary checking, reversed two venues, generated more than a dozen corrections, and required a next-day correction. The operating response is assigned stories, editing, source checks, ESP upload, and a final read-aloud review, not simply buying additional subscribers. Sharpe likewise says expansion depends on suitable journalist partners and adequate runway; finding the right people is difficult, and smaller markets can bring higher acquisition costs and slower revenue. Office Party encountered another ceiling: year-end advertiser budgets slowed demand, while twice-weekly publishing limited inventory. Parker and Sakamoto would explore owned products or services earlier, although their limited time makes service delivery unattractive. Sneddon's revenue distinction belongs in the same economics check: $350,000 was the interview-year target, while the previous year produced $200,000. The projected value of unsold inventory and possible events was not money already collected. These accounts place staffing, accuracy, sales work, and inventory alongside acquisition in the operating picture. chapters.question_prompt: What disclosure and endorsement issues do these practitioners and legal presenters identify, and what rules and risks arise when advertisers use brand names?
chapters.title: Affiliate Disclosures, Endorsements, and Brand-Name Advertising
chapters.subtitle: FTC disclosure placement, YouTube affiliate links and sponsorships, social-media endorsements, Amazon disclosures, proposed and updated endorsement guidance, and competitor-brand advertising disputes.
chapters.executive_summary: The recurring practitioner position is straightforward: explain the relationship, put the explanation beside the recommendation, and support the claims being sold. Erika Kullberg demonstrates commission language beside YouTube links; Michael Ostheimer identifies 'paid link' as a two-word option and matches disclosures to visual and audio endorsements. Carmen layers Amazon identification with individual post disclosures. Placement remains contested: Cheryl Phan and Alston Godbolt describe bottom-of-content approaches, while other presenters reject buried notices. Hustle Audit reports a $15.2 million Teami judgment partially suspended to a $1 million payment. On brand advertising, Grow My Ads favors direct contact over escalation; Analytics Playbook separates competitor keywords from visible ad copy and warns about higher click costs and automated name insertion.

key_metrics.label: Compact affiliate-link disclosure
key_metrics.context: Michael Ostheimer identifies 'paid link' directly beside an affiliate link as adequate language describing the nature of that link.

key_metrics.label: Influencer and brand reminder letters
key_metrics.context: Brian Heidelberger reports letters to celebrities, athletes, other influencers, and brands reminding them to disclose material connections.

key_metrics.label: Teami judgment and payment
key_metrics.context: Hustle Audit reports the March 2020 settlement as a judgment partially suspended to a payment reflecting what the company could pay.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Start with the relationship, not the hashtag. Tom Cohen's baseline at AM Days is truthful, substantiated product claims plus disclosure when an affiliate receives money or payment in kind. The connection can run through an advertiser or a network; receiving commissions for traffic does not put the publisher outside the problem. Cohen also separates an ordinary endorsement from deceptive packaging: fake news articles, fake blogs, and fake review sites are formats they specifically warn against [0ELJUfzzK1M @ 00:00:15]. Justin Moore makes the same relationship test concrete for creators. Cash is only one possibility. A free product, a hotel stay, a trip, or an event-ticket upgrade tied to a social post can all supply something of value. Moore's practical preference in uncertain situations is to disclose rather than argue over whether the perk counts [oQhn2MkCyK4 @ 00:01:24]. Lawyer Kae describes the trigger as an unexpected material relationship, including financial, family, and work connections. Their audience test asks whether knowing about the relationship would change the weight viewers give the recommendation. The shared business mechanic is therefore broader than an affiliate URL: the audience needs to understand a connection that could affect the credibility of the endorsement [9bddsIKkfe0 @ 00:02:53].

The recurring placement standard is notice without a hunt. Erika Kullberg demonstrates a working affiliate disclosure beside the link and contrasts it with a link at the top of a YouTube description whose explanation sits at the bottom. Their objection is proximity: viewers should see the link and the commission explanation together, not infer that a distant block of text applies to an earlier URL. Kullberg also rejects 'affiliate link' alone because viewers outside the creator business may not understand the expression [723U5nGxhTU @ 00:05:55]. Tricia Meyer describes why the word 'unavoidable' matters in day-to-day affiliate work. People do not necessarily finish a post, watch a video to its end, or open all the comments. Their interpretation requires the disclosure to accompany the review, video, or sponsored image that the person actually consumes [ny2He3BVEgM @ 00:08:22]. Hustle Audit reaches the same operational distinction through failed placements: an ad tag after a pile of hashtags, a notice behind 'more,' and tiny gray text against a busy background can exist without communicating anything useful. Their test is whether an ordinary audience member would notice and understand the relationship, rather than whether the publisher can point to a disclosure somewhere [3FcVWGZ_SGY @ 00:01:31].

Disclosure does not replace evidence for the recommendation. John Norling of Jennings Strouss says advertisers need backup for their claims and must convey material buying information clearly. They reject fine print at the bottom and rapid-fire audio that listeners cannot understand. The presentation treats truthfulness, supporting evidence, and readable delivery as connected advertising duties, not interchangeable fixes [zMHcPlc6Nvc @ 00:06:11]. Venable's Alex McGarry and Len Gordon explain the same separation through testimonials: endorsements must reflect genuine opinions or experience, come from actual users when represented that way, and not distort the endorser's view through editing. A product claim does not become supportable merely because a customer says it instead of the advertiser [BY7l2XbdWPc @ 00:03:36]. Responsibility also extends beyond the person appearing on camera. Michael Ostheimer says advertisers should give endorsers guidance, monitor their conduct, and take action that remedies problems and prevents recurrence. Their discussion includes advertiser exposure for misleading or unsubstantiated statements and missing unexpected connections, even where the endorser is not liable. The baseline program is therefore education followed by actual observation and correction, rather than simply paying a creator and assuming the published result will explain itself [Hq1UDKzazVQ @ 00:12:31].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Use the short scripts the presenters actually demonstrate. Kullberg's affiliate example explains that they may receive a commission if the viewer clicks the link. For sponsorships, their examples identify the sponsor directly or explain that a named company supplied the review product free. When reviewing several products, they say to identify the connection for each free item, rather than treating one general acknowledgment as a description of every relationship [723U5nGxhTU @ 00:03:34]. Ostheimer supplies an even shorter link-level option: place 'paid link' right next to the affiliate link. They call this adequate disclosure of the link's nature and emphasize that it takes only two words [Hq1UDKzazVQ @ 00:28:18]. Carmen, publishing as eternalsoulwriter, separates Amazon's account identification from individual link disclosures. They quote 'As an Amazon associate, I earn from qualifying purchases' and say they retain Amazon's wording. Their examples of link-level labels include #ad, #CommissionsEarned, and 'paid link.' A visible website statement or a social account bio is an additional location, not a replacement for disclosures on individual affiliate posts. That distinction is central to Carmen's workflow: identify the Amazon relationship at account level while still explaining the commercial connection where the audience encounters the particular promotion [5myKyThXemw @ 00:03:13].

Match the delivery to how the endorsement is consumed. Ostheimer says visual claims need visual disclosures, audible claims need audible disclosures, and endorsements delivered both ways need both. Visual text should stand apart from accompanying elements; spoken wording needs a volume, speed, and cadence that ordinary listeners can understand. Their examples also reject an execution that works on a computer but fails on a smartphone [Hq1UDKzazVQ @ 00:10:30]. Digital Trailblazer's LeahRae applies this to an affiliate software tutorial: say in the video that the link can generate commissions. Their additional YouTube mechanic is an upload-default disclosure, so the channel's videos receive a recurring description notice. They explain that their default sits lower down, while a direct review receives another disclosure higher in the description to avoid scrolling [EJWC8jVfIko @ 00:02:12]. Carmen extends the same repeated-placement approach across their own publishing stack. They put a disclosure near the beginning of affiliate blog articles, use YouTube's about section and video descriptions, and maintain a dedicated Linktree disclosure section before visitors reach affiliate links. Their Facebook routine adds notices in the page bio, affiliate-post descriptions, and comments. These are Carmen's reported additional placements, alongside their endorsement of spoken and visual video disclosures [5myKyThXemw @ 00:08:12].

For competitor advertising, Analytics Playbook separates campaign targeting from the words displayed in the ad. Their testing sequence starts with a separate competitor campaign to control spend and track performance, followed by a comparison landing page and copy focused on differentiators such as support or pricing. They favor competitors resembling the advertiser rather than a giant with a much larger budget. Their two automation checks are explicit: do not use dynamic keyword insertion, and turn off automatically created assets that could pull a competitor's name into ad copy [HMW_yXXlRPs @ 00:01:48]. Grow My Ads handles the reverse situation with direct outreach. Their first move is to find the advertiser's contact details, use email or LinkedIn, and send a screenshot showing the ad and search term. The message allows for an agency mistake or a dynamic search ad rather than opening with accusations; it asks for removal of the brand name from that ad and other affected ads [PQ6b58aTlas @ 00:01:21]. Brian Heidelberger applies similarly specific instructions to influencer relationships: agree in advance what disclosure the creator will use. They say a bare instruction to follow FTC requirements leaves too much room for the creator to choose wording that fails [1g3rmmIH9VM @ 00:03:56].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Bottom-of-content practices are the sharpest placement conflict. Cheryl Phan says they put commission language at the bottom of blog posts and also maintain website policies. Their sample explains that affiliate links make shopping easier and that commissions may come from companies mentioned in the post. Later, Phan also insists the notice must be obvious, easy to see, and require no scrolling. Those instructions sit alongside their repeated description of bottom placement, rather than resolving when the bottom will actually be visible [fnCkagoHXx0 @ 00:02:27]. Alston Godbolt favors a website disclosure, mentions a blurb at the bottom of YouTube content, and describes using a footer or a website widget area. They simultaneously read out the requirement that electronic disclosures be unavoidable and not buried in long captions or hashtags [TpYEmQ9njyk @ 00:03:31]. Kullberg's demonstrated alternative is more restrictive about location: a link at the top and disclosure at the bottom do not work together because viewers may never see the explanation or connect it to the URL. Their approach keeps the commission statement very close to the actual link. These are different publishing instructions, not equivalent ways of implementing the same physical placement [723U5nGxhTU @ 00:06:15].

Wording and repeat disclosure also produce genuine differences. Phan says the notice must begin with the word 'disclosure' and offers language about commissions from the companies mentioned. That is a specific wording prescription, not merely a suggestion to explain the relationship [fnCkagoHXx0 @ 00:02:10]. Lawyer Kae takes the opposite position on a mandatory opening: there is no special FTC language, provided the essential relationship information is clear. Their examples identify who paid for a trip, gifted a product, or sponsored a video. They also warn against omitting part of the arrangement, such as describing a free product while leaving out an additional payment [9bddsIKkfe0 @ 00:08:38]. On continuing product use, Kae says creators should continue revealing that the company originally provided the item because new viewers encounter later content [9bddsIKkfe0 @ 00:13:32]. Ostheimer gives a narrower, context-dependent alternative. In their example, someone still genuinely enjoying a free video game a year later may no longer need to disclose that old gift. For a person who subsequently buys more product, they distinguish an ongoing brand relationship from a past gift without continuing ties. Their explanation turns on audience expectations and continuing relationships, not an automatic perpetual notice for every later mention [Hq1UDKzazVQ @ 00:34:15].

The legal presenters also distinguish proposals and interpretations from a self-executing penalty schedule. Venable explicitly describes its endorsement-guides discussion as proposed changes and explains that the guides are advisory: an enforcement action still requires establishing deceptive or unfair conduct. Their discussion of potential future enforcement is framed around what the commission might do, not a report that every proposed example has already produced a penalty [BY7l2XbdWPc @ 00:02:56]. Ostheimer likewise says the updated guides are interpretations rather than regulations, and that the commission still has to prove unfairness or deception [Hq1UDKzazVQ @ 00:03:51]. Brand-name advertising has its own important separation. Analytics Playbook says competitor names can be keywords while visible use in ad copy can draw a trademark complaint; their presentation describes Google's response as advertiser-specific and discusses an authorized-reseller exception as of February 2025 [HMW_yXXlRPs @ 00:00:43]. Grow My Ads focuses instead on getting a displayed name removed: contact the advertiser first, then consider Google's trademark complaint route when the brand owns a trademark. Their fallback without one is an ad report, which they describe as slower and harder. A keyword campaign and a complaint about displayed copy are therefore different situations in these presenters' playbooks [PQ6b58aTlas @ 00:02:36].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The firsthand breakdowns are often mundane rather than elaborate. Phan openly says they forgot a disclosure themselves, despite trying to make it a routine part of blogging. They also say nobody has contacted them about it; that is their personal experience, not a measured enforcement outcome for other creators [fnCkagoHXx0 @ 00:00:16]. Carmen describes struggling to find other creators' notices buried among hashtags and identifies different platform character limits as a frustration in their own disclosure workflow. Their response is repeated placement across accounts, posts, captions, and Linktree, rather than relying on visitors to hunt down a single account statement [5myKyThXemw @ 00:11:40]. Grow My Ads supplies a direct advertising mistake from its own work: dynamic search ads accidentally included competitors' names in client advertisements. The competitor complained to the client, the client asked the agency what was happening, and the agency explained and corrected the issue. The presenter says that in roughly a decade in the industry, none of their clients actually needed to hire a lawyer for these disputes. Their reported experience supports starting with contact and correction, while leaving the separate Google reporting routes available when the advertiser does not respond [PQ6b58aTlas @ 00:03:57].

Keep reported enforcement cases separate from presenters' own operational losses. Hustle Audit describes Teami's March 2020 settlement as a $15.2 million judgment partially suspended to a $1 million payment reflecting ability to pay. Their account combines unsupported health claims with influencer posts that buried the paid relationship, followed by warning letters to ten influencers. The placement lesson they extract is specific: disclosures belong above 'more' and outside a clump of hashtags [3FcVWGZ_SGY @ 00:04:12]. Kae discusses the same brand's enforcement history as an example involving scientific support, endorser monitoring, and ongoing reports, not simply a missing label. Their explanation also identifies legal response costs and possible surrender of money connected with violations [9bddsIKkfe0 @ 00:05:38]. Meyer points to Legacy Learning Systems as another reported case where undisclosed affiliate payments produced continuing administrative obligations. Their emphasis is the work after the dispute: recordkeeping, notifications, closer scrutiny, and additional processes imposed on the retailer. None of those presenters describes these company judgments as their own personal loss. The economics they identify include both money exposed in an enforcement action and the continuing operational burden of having to document and report future conduct [ny2He3BVEgM @ 00:11:27].

The harder economics check is whether the business can support the claim it wants to advertise. Venable describes firsthand disputes with the FTC over earnings-claim substantiation: tracking every purchaser's results is difficult when companies lack monitoring mechanisms and customers apply training with different levels of diligence. Gordon describes this as an ongoing fight in cases, not a settled permission to advertise any impressive result. They also tell marketers to avoid claims that the process is easy or that everybody makes money [BY7l2XbdWPc @ 00:46:10]. Cohen's operational warning is similarly direct: do not copy network or advertiser material and assume the product claims are substantiated. Testimonials and before-and-after pictures need to be real and documented, with supporting evidence on file before publication [0ELJUfzzK1M @ 00:06:27]. Paid search introduces a different cost problem. Analytics Playbook says competitor keywords almost always carry higher click costs and may have little volume in niche markets [HMW_yXXlRPs @ 00:00:15]. They also warn that putting a competitor's name in visible copy can bring confused visitors who expected the other company and leave immediately. Their recommended comparison page and differentiating copy address that mismatch rather than treating a competitor's brand name as automatically valuable traffic [HMW_yXXlRPs @ 00:01:31].

callout.title: Practitioner checks before the next promotion
callout.body: Use the presenters' own failure checks: evidence, actual visibility, automated copy, and support for outcome claims.
items: Check that testimonials, before-and-after pictures, and product claims are real and documented; Cohen says not to assume advertiser or network copy already has the necessary support. [AM Days — 0ELJUfzzK1M @ 00:06:27]

Check the smartphone presentation, not only the desktop version. Ostheimer says a disclosure that is clear on a computer is insufficient when it is not clear on a phone. [Find Your Influence — Hq1UDKzazVQ @ 00:11:57]

Check whether dynamic search ads have inserted competitor names into visible copy; Grow My Ads reports correcting that exact mistake after competitors complained to clients. [Grow My Ads — PQ6b58aTlas @ 00:04:15]
For earnings claims, check the result-tracking burden Gordon describes and remove claims that everybody makes money or that the process is easy. [Venable LLP — BY7l2XbdWPc @ 00:47:25]

chapters.pull_quote: "You can't just take something directly from your network or your advertiser and assume that it all contains true substantiated product claims." — Tom Cohen, AM Days (0ELJUfzzK1M @ 00:06:27).
action_checklist: Identify the exchanged value behind the endorsement, including free products, travel, hotel stays, and conditional upgrades rather than cash alone. [Justin Moore — oQhn2MkCyK4 @ 00:01:24]
Place plain commission language beside the affiliate link, where viewers can see both together. [Lawyer Explains - Erika Kullberg — 723U5nGxhTU @ 00:05:55]
Match disclosures to visual and audible endorsements, and make on-screen text distinct and spoken wording understandable. [Find Your Influence — Hq1UDKzazVQ @ 00:10:30]

Retain Amazon account identification while also disclosing individual affiliate posts; Carmen explicitly says account-level disclosure does not replace post-level disclosure. [eternalsoulwriter — 5myKyThXemw @ 00:04:35]
Agree on the actual disclosure language with creators before posting instead of relying on a general instruction to follow requirements. [Brian Heidelberger — 1g3rmmIH9VM @ 00:03:56]

Separate competitor campaigns for spending and performance review, build comparison landing pages, and prevent automated insertion of competitor names into copy. [Analytics Playbook: Learn Marketing Analytics — HMW_yXXlRPs @ 00:01:48] [Analytics Playbook: Learn Marketing Analytics — HMW_yXXlRPs @ 00:02:22]
